analysis.one_liner: Requires firearms to be stored securely and lifts gun makers' legal shield from lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee, then a subcommittee, from July 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, with only four cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to keep an unsecured firearm — one without a lock or safe — and would let people injured by an unsecured gun sue the owner, or anyone controlling the property, for damages. It would also repeal the 2005 law that shields gun makers and dealers from most lawsuits over criminal misuse of their products, and make federal gun-trace data usable as evidence in civil cases. Finally, it would set up federal grants for states and tribes that adopt matching safe-storage laws. None of this went anywhere: the House Judiciary Committee never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Families harmed by guns left unsecured — including children who find a loaded gun — would gain a new right to sue the careless owner and the person controlling the property for compensatory and punitive damages. Shooting victims and municipalities could also bring suits against manufacturers and dealers that the current liability shield blocks, using ATF trace data as evidence. States and tribes that pass matching safe-storage laws would get federal grant money to enforce them.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful to keep or store any unsecured firearm, defined as one not secured by a safe or safety device, unless the owner is carrying it or can readily retrieve it [S2][S3].

It creates a private right of action: anyone injured by an unsecured gun — or, if they died, their family or estate — can sue the violator and anyone in control of the premises who knew or should have known about it, for compensatory and punitive damages, with joint and several liability [S3].

It repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the 2005 statute that blocks most civil suits against gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations over criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm [S2][S3].
It removes the immunity of the ATF's Firearms Trace System database, making gun-trace data subject to subpoena, discoverable, and admissible in civil suits and administrative proceedings [S2][S3].

It directs the Justice Department to award grants to states and Indian tribes that enact functionally identical safe-storage laws, to help law enforcement and courts enforce compliance, and gives those states preference in other Justice Department grants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, dealers, and trade associations would lose the 2005 federal shield that has protected them from suits over criminal misuse of their products, and would face suits supported by ATF trace data. Individual gun owners would bear a new legal duty to lock up firearms, backed by criminal penalties and exposure to damages claims, and property owners could face liability for unsecured guns on premises they control. Taxpayers would fund the state and tribal enforcement grants and annual reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun industry, gun owners, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The storage mandate is a flat federal offense: an otherwise law-abiding owner who leaves a gun unsecured with no one harmed has still committed a crime, raising concerns about overreach into lawful gun ownership [S3].

The private right of action is broad: it reaches not just the owner but any person who controlled the premises — a landlord, relative, or spouse — who 'knew or should have known' an unsecured gun was there, with joint and several liability and punitive damages, which could sweep in people with only indirect connection to the firearm [S3].

Repealing the manufacturer liability shield would expose an entire lawful industry to litigation over third-party criminal acts, which industry backers argue threatens dealers and makers who played no role in the misuse [S2].

The bill itself requires an annual Justice Department report breaking down enforcement by race, sex, age, and ethnicity — an acknowledgment in the bill's own text that enforcement of firearms offenses can fall unevenly across groups [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is real: unsecured guns are a major source of child shootings, thefts, and suicides, and both the storage mandate and the lawsuits give owners a concrete financial reason to lock firearms up. The cost side is also real — the storage offense and the wide premises-liability and punitive-damages claims could penalize people who caused no harm, and reopening litigation against manufacturers over third-party crimes is a major, deliberate shift against the gun industry. The bill is more aggressive than a typical 'lock your gun' law because it pairs the mandate with the industry-shield repeal; a narrower version keeping only storage plus grants would be easier to defend, and its enforceability against tens of millions of households is a fair question.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, sent to a crime subcommittee more than a year later, and died there when the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald McEachin introduced the Firearm Owners Responsibility and Safety Act on July 29, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
On November 1, 2022, more than a year after introduction, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
The committee never held a hearing or markup and the House never voted on it; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations, who kept the 2005 liability shield the bill would have repealed; individual gun owners also avoided the new storage mandate. No one gained the bill's protections for families harmed by unsecured guns.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill would repeal the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which since 2005 has blocked most civil suits against the industry over criminal misuse of firearms, and would make ATF trace data usable against manufacturers and dealers in court. The industry's core legal shield was the bill's main target, and gun industry groups have long opposed its repeal.

The bill requires insurers to treat a safe-storage violation as more than an intentional act when interpreting policies, limiting insurers' ability to deny claims for storage-related shootings as intentional conduct; this makes it harder to deny such claims but also clarifies exposure on an otherwise-undefined issue.
